notes.meaning: God visited Sarah with mercy and gave her the strength to conceive, just as He had told Abraham before. He kept His word at the exact time He had set, showing that His promises never fail. When God steps in, He changes human lives according to His faithful plan.

Sarah became pregnant and gave birth to a son for Abraham in his old age. This birth did not happen by the ordinary laws of nature, because both parents were far too old. It happened entirely through a miracle of God's grace at the exact time He had promised.

Abraham obeyed God by naming his new baby Isaac, which means laughter. When Abraham and Sarah first heard God's promise of a child, they had laughed in shock and doubt. Now God turned that name into an announcement of real, lasting joy for their household.

Abraham circumcised Isaac when the baby was eight days old, exactly as God commanded. Circumcision was the outward mark showing that Isaac belonged to God's special covenant agreement. Abraham did not delay this painful duty, showing his prompt obedience to God's word.

Abraham was one hundred years old when Isaac was born. His great age highlighted how powerless human effort was to bring about the promised son. The birth proved that the blessings of the covenant come purely by God's supernatural power.

Sarah declared that God had filled her heart with genuine laughter and joy. She knew that anyone who heard about this wonderful birth would be amazed and celebrate with her. God delights to give His people joy that goes far beyond anything they expected.

Sarah marveled that an elderly woman like her was actually nursing a baby for Abraham. Nobody would have believed such news unless God Himself had spoken and done it. In her joy, Sarah also remembered her past unbelief and gave all praise to God's power.

Isaac grew healthy and was weaned, which usually took place when a child was around two or three years old. Abraham held a large feast to thank God for protecting the boy through the dangers of infancy. Celebrating milestones with gratitude reminds us of God's tender care.

During the feast, Sarah saw Ishmael mocking young Isaac. Ishmael was a teenager who made fun of the little child and belittled God's promise about Isaac's future role. This bitter ridicule showed real disrespect toward the child of promise.

differ.view: Ishmael's mocking was a spiteful act of scorn against God's promise and Isaac, amounting to spiritual persecution.
The dispute was likely over who would get the family inheritance, and Ishmael may have even fought physically with Isaac.
The mocking was probably just light teasing or playful ridicule about Sarah's old age rather than malice.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The word can simply mean playing, which suggests Sarah was offended merely by seeing Ishmael near her son.

notes.meaning: Sarah told Abraham to expel Hagar and Ishmael so that Ishmael would not share the family inheritance with Isaac. She wanted to protect Isaac's place as the sole heir of God's covenant blessings. Though Sarah spoke out of personal anger, her words fit God's greater plan to separate the covenant line.

differ.view: The two women represent two kinds of righteousness and the two testaments, showing that human works cannot earn God's blessing.
Hagar represents the covenant of works, showing that no one can receive God's promise or be saved by keeping the law.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Hagar represents the old earthly Jewish synagogue, while Sarah represents the church of the Gentiles.

notes.meaning: Sarah's demand caused Abraham deep distress because Ishmael was his own son. Abraham loved the boy and was pained by his bad behavior, but he was also grieved by how harsh it seemed to banish him. Broken family relationships bring real sorrow to a godly heart.

God spoke to Abraham and told him not to be distressed, but to listen to what Sarah said. God explained that Abraham's true covenant family and the promised Savior would be traced strictly through Isaac. God's choice of Isaac showed that the covenant depended on divine promise rather than birth order.

God comforted Abraham by promising that Ishmael would also become the founder of a great nation. Even though Ishmael was excluded from the covenant line, God did not abandon him. God gave Ishmael earthly blessings simply because he was Abraham's son.

Abraham woke up early, placed bread and a skin of water on Hagar's shoulder, and sent her away with Ishmael. Hagar wandered into the wilderness of Beersheba and lost her way. Abraham acted in painful but prompt obedience to God's direct command.

differ.view: Abraham gave very meager supplies, obeying God's command half-heartedly because he was so grieved.
Abraham gave what was customary for a journey to the next well, trusting God entirely to take care of them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Abraham sent them off with minimal provisions because Hagar's low status as an enslaved woman gave her no rights.

notes.meaning: The supply of water ran out in the desert heat, and Ishmael collapsed from thirst and exhaustion. Hagar placed her weakened son under the shade of a bush so he would not bake in the sun. Without any water left, death seemed only a matter of time.

Hagar walked about a bowshot away and broke down in tears because she could not bear to watch her son die. In her extreme grief, she forgot God's past promise that Ishmael would grow up to have a large family. Trouble can easily make people lose sight of God's promises.

God heard the cries of Ishmael lying under the bush in the desert. An angel called to Hagar from heaven and told her not to be afraid because God knew exactly where the boy was. God hears the cries of those who are suffering, even in the loneliest places.

The angel told Hagar to get up, lift the boy, and hold him by the hand. God repeated His promise that Ishmael would become a great nation. This promise gave Hagar the hope and courage she needed to keep caring for her son.

God opened Hagar's eyes so that she saw a well of water nearby. She filled her empty water skin and gave the boy a drink, saving his life. Often God's help is closer than people realize, but they need Him to open their eyes to see it.

God watched over the boy as he grew up, giving him health and protection in the wilderness. Ishmael learned how to hunt and defend himself, becoming a skilled archer. His ability to survive and prosper was the direct result of God's kind providence.

Ishmael made his home in the desert of Paran, in northern Arabia. His mother followed ancient family custom by choosing a wife for him from her homeland of Egypt. Even in the wilderness, family life was maintained under God's guidance.

King Abimelech and his army commander, Phicol, came to talk with Abraham. They openly recognized that God was with Abraham and blessed everything he did. When a believer lives faithfully, even worldly neighbors and leaders notice God's favor.

Abimelech asked Abraham to swear an oath before God that he would treat the king, his children, and his land with honesty. The king pointed out that he had treated Abraham well and expected the same loyalty in return. God's people should always be fair and return the kindness shown to them.

Abraham agreed right away to swear the oath. He knew that making a peaceful agreement in God's name was proper and lawful. Believers should be willing to promote peace with their neighbors whenever they can.

Before completing the treaty, Abraham complained to Abimelech about a water well that the king's servants had seized. Water was extremely precious in that dry region, and Abraham had worked hard to dig the well. It is wise to clear up past wrongs honestly before making a new agreement.

Abimelech answered that he had no idea his servants had taken the well and was only hearing about it now. Abraham accepted his explanation, recognizing that leaders do not always know about the wrong things their servants do. Honest people are glad to listen and correct misunderstandings.

Abraham gave sheep and cattle to Abimelech, and the two men entered into a formal covenant of peace. A covenant was a serious, binding promise made between two parties. Giving these valuable animals was an ancient way to seal a firm friendship.

Abraham set apart seven female lambs from the rest of the flock. By putting these animals to the side, he showed that a special matter needed to be settled alongside their general treaty. He was preparing to resolve the dispute about the well.

Abimelech asked Abraham what the seven separate lambs were for. The king wanted to know what this extra gift meant before he agreed to it. Wise people ask questions to make sure the terms of an agreement are completely clear.

Abraham explained that Abimelech's acceptance of the seven lambs would serve as proof that Abraham had dug the well. Taking the gift meant the king officially recognized Abraham's legal right to the water. Making agreements clear helps avoid future arguments.

The place was named Beersheba, which means either the well of the oath or the well of seven. Both men took a solemn oath there to keep their agreement. The name served as a lasting reminder of the honest promises they made to each other.

After making their covenant at Beersheba, Abimelech and Phicol returned home to the land of the Philistines. The agreement settled their borders and brought safety to Abraham's household. God gave His servant a season of quiet and peace after many years of wandering.

Abraham planted a tamarisk tree at Beersheba and worshiped the Lord, the Eternal God. Planting a slow-growing tree showed he felt secure and trusted God's long-term promise to give his family the land. Abraham made sure to practice and share his faith openly wherever he lived.

Abraham stayed in the land of the Philistines for a long time as a sojourner. Even though he had a peaceful place to live, he remembered that he was still a traveler waiting for God's full promise to come true. Believers can enjoy God's earthly blessings while remembering that heaven is their true home.
